title: Immunology: innate and adaptive defenses, antibodies and vaccines
note: Innate immunity responds within minutes to patterns shared by many microbes but has no memory. Adaptive immunity, carried out by B cells (antibodies) and T cells, is specific and slower the first time, but it leaves memory cells. Vaccines exploit that memory by presenting antigen safely before a real infection.

read.title: How a vaccine trains the immune system
text: The first time the adaptive immune system meets a new antigen, the response is slow. Only a few B and T cells happen to have receptors that fit, and they must be selected, activated and multiplied before they can clear the threat. Antibody levels take days to rise, and IgM appears first.

This first encounter leaves behind long-lived memory B and T cells. On a later exposure they respond faster and more strongly, producing higher levels of antibody, mostly IgG. That faster secondary response is the whole point of a vaccine: it supplies the first encounter safely, so the dangerous one meets a prepared defense.

Vaccines differ in what they present. Live attenuated vaccines use a weakened organism that still replicates, which tends to give strong, lasting immunity but is not suitable for some people with weakened immune systems. Inactivated vaccines use killed organisms. Subunit and conjugate vaccines present only key antigens, and toxoids present a harmless form of a bacterial toxin. mRNA vaccines deliver instructions so the body's own cells briefly make an antigen. Many vaccines include an adjuvant, an ingredient that strengthens the response, and immunity takes weeks to develop after a dose.

q.q: Why is the first adaptive response to an antigen slow?
o: Few matching lymphocytes exist and must be activated and multiplied
